title: Spokane Shows What the New Era of Wildfires Looks Like
gist: Three wildfires around Spokane destroyed more than 700 buildings in roughly two days, part of a Pacific Northwest season in which Oregon broke its annual acreage record at nearly 2 million acres and Washington logged its most destructive season on record with over half a million acres burned and at least 65,000 residents evacuated. Sources tie the outbreak to a historically small snowpack that melted early, a warming atmosphere that dries fuels, and the wildland-urban interface — the fastest-growing US land development type — whose cul-de-sac street layouts trapped evacuees in traffic.

themes.theme: Scale of the 2026 Pacific Northwest season

insights.claim: Oregon broke its annual record for acreage burned with nearly 2 million acres scorched while still early in the fire season, after a historically dry winter, extreme drought and heat waves.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Record acreage set before the seasonal peak implies the annual loss figure that insurers and reinsurers price against is materially understated at mid-season.
insights.locator: A historically dry winter, extreme drought, and heat waves

insights.claim: Washington is in its most destructive fire season on record with more than half a million acres burned and at least 65,000 residents ordered to evacuate statewide.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Mass evacuation on this scale drives emergency housing, utility shutoff and municipal credit questions well beyond the burn footprint itself.
insights.locator: Washington is also in the middle of its most destructive season on record

insights.claim: Three large fires that started Saturday around Spokane had destroyed more than 700 buildings by Monday afternoon, turning the Spokane Convention Center into a Red Cross emergency shelter for hundreds of evacuees.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Structure loss concentrated into ~48 hours is the loss profile that overwhelms claims processing and local rebuilding capacity simultaneously.
insights.locator: The three large fires that started on Saturday around Spokane

insights.claim: Despite the destruction, a Spokane City Council member said no fatalities and no missing people were known as of Tuesday morning, while many of the displaced are senior citizens and their caretakers.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: A property-loss-heavy, casualty-light event shifts the burden onto insurance and long-term senior housing rather than emergency medical response.
insights.quote: It’s a miracle that, so far, we know of no fatalities and no reported missing people
insights.locator: I’ve been trying to wrap my mind around how we’re going to house all these folks

insights.claim: A Red Cross communications director with 10 years at the organization who has seen prior wildfire disasters says the scale of homes destroyed is a new level, and that the organization is bracing for seasons that get worse and start earlier and end later.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: A lengthening fire season compresses the off-season used for mitigation work and raises the annualized cost of standing firefighting and relief capacity.
insights.quote: We are bracing ourselves for seasons like this getting worse and worse, and starting earlier and going later.
insights.locator: Robertson, a communications director for the Red Cross

themes.theme: Snowpack failure as the proximate driver

insights.claim: AccuWeather senior meteorologist Paul Pastelok attributes the fire setup to a lack of regional snowfall: snowpack normally melts gradually and supplies steady moisture, but this year an already-small pack was hit by hot spring temperatures and melted early, leaving the landscape parched.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Winter snowpack readings become a leading indicator for summer fire risk — a monitorable variable months ahead of the loss event.
insights.locator: According to Paul Pastelok, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather

insights.claim: Spokane received half its typical snowfall this year and other parts of Washington received even less, with many areas reaching historic lows.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Quantifies the precursor deficit — a 50 percent snowfall shortfall preceded a record destruction season, a usable rule of thumb for forward risk.
insights.locator: Spokane had half of the typical snowfall this year

insights.claim: A warmer atmosphere holds about 7 percent more water vapor per 1 degree Celsius of warming, pulling moisture out of soils and vegetation and leaving forests and grasslands primed to burn, while also making rain fall more intensely but less frequently and lengthening droughts.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: The Clausius-Clapeyron relationship is the physical mechanism converting warming into fuel dryness — it makes fire-loss escalation a trend rather than a run of bad luck.
insights.locator: As the planet heats up, the conditions that fuel extreme wildfires

insights.claim: Bob Freitag, recently director of the Institute of Hazards Mitigation Research and Planning at the University of Washington, says the fire and what is expected to come make no sense except as a consequence of a changing climate and that this is not a one-off.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Expert framing of the event as structural rather than anomalous is what shifts actuarial models from historical averages to trend extrapolation.
insights.quote: This fire, and what we’re expecting to come, makes no sense unless you connect the dots through a changing climate

insights.claim: Powerful winds carried hot embers from the 70,000-acre Little Giant fire in central Washington more than 3 miles, jumping the flames clear across Lake Chelan into forests on the far side.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Three-mile ember transport over open water defeats firebreak-based containment assumptions, widening the exposure radius used in risk mapping.
insights.locator: In the past few days, powerful winds carried hot embers

themes.theme: Wildland-urban interface as the loss multiplier

insights.claim: Suburban development in the wildland-urban interface, where homes mingle with natural areas, is the fastest growing type of land development in the United States, and research shows homes built there are more likely to burn when wildfires spread.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: The exposed housing stock is growing faster than the average, so aggregate wildfire loss rises even holding fire behavior constant — a structural driver of homeowner insurance repricing and withdrawal.
insights.locator: Areas where homes mingle with natural areas

insights.claim: Street layout is an underrated loss factor: winding cul-de-sac neighborhoods with thousands of residents and only two ways in or out slowed evacuations, trapped residents in traffic for hours, and impeded emergency responders reaching the fires.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Road-network egress capacity is a measurable, parcel-level risk variable that current underwriting largely ignores — a candidate for the next wave of catastrophe modeling.
insights.quote: These are neighborhoods with thousands of people and only two ways in or out
insights.locator: Klitzke, the city council member, said the affected neighborhoods

insights.claim: Steep terrain and abundant plant life in the affected Spokane neighborhoods let the fires spread quickly over the weekend, and the council member says the vulnerability was already known before the fires.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Known-but-unmitigated hazard is a litigation and municipal-liability pattern that tends to surface after high-loss fire events.
insights.quote: We already knew that this was a dangerous situation
insights.locator: Klitzke, the city council member, said the affected neighborhoods in Spokane

insights.claim: Fire-prone states such as California increasingly require homeowners to clear trees and shrubs in a radius around the home, a defensible space buffer that can dramatically reduce the chance a wildfire ignites a building.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Defensible-space mandates spreading beyond California create compliance costs for homeowners and a service market for vegetation management contractors.
insights.locator: Increasingly, fire-prone states like California are requiring homeowners

insights.claim: A California wildfire public information officer notes the core adoption problem for defensible space is that residents chose these neighborhoods precisely because they love the vegetation they are now asked to remove.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Voluntary mitigation will underperform because the mitigation destroys the amenity people paid for — expect mandates and insurance pricing, not persuasion, to do the work.
insights.quote: But we can’t live in that world anymore because of these fires.
insights.locator: People chose to live in these neighborhoods precisely because they love the vegetation

themes.theme: Urban smoke toxicity and the LA 2025 analogue

insights.claim: A wildfire public information officer says the Spokane situation is comparable to the 2025 Los Angeles fires because both began in wild areas before moving into partially forested suburban neighborhoods, and the urban setting makes the resulting smoke especially toxic.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: When fires consume built structures rather than only vegetation, health exposure becomes a separate and larger liability channel than property loss.
insights.locator: The situation is comparable to the Los Angeles fires in 2025

insights.claim: A recently released study found the Los Angeles fires, which sent more than 200,000 residents fleeing, exposed an estimated 3.3 million people to high concentrations of a cancer-causing toxin.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: A 16-to-1 ratio of toxin-exposed people to evacuees shows the health footprint dwarfs the evacuation zone — the basis for future mass health claims and air-filtration demand.
insights.locator: A recently released study found that the Los Angeles fires

insights.claim: The Washington Department of Natural Resources describes the season as exceptionally challenging for the thousands of wildland firefighters deployed across the state, with more high winds forecast for the weekend that could worsen conditions in Spokane.
insights.speaker: Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
insights.so_what: Firefighting workforce strain plus forecast wind events is the setup for containment failure — the near-term variable determining whether losses double again.
insights.locator: Ryan Rodruck, a communications manager at the Washington Department of Natural Resources
